name: Anthony Weaver

views.text: Coach players hard and then love them up; both halves matter.
A former player knows what a setback feels like and can talk a player through it.
Players see things on the field the booth cannot, so ask them how the calls should be taught.
Look for tough, competitive players first; scheme comes second.
Fourth-quarter collapses come from habits, and habits are fixed by repetition, not blame.
An opponent should walk off the field feeling it has been in a fight.
Running the room while the head coach calls the game is a real job, and ego has no place in it.
A defense that is having fun plays faster and celebrates for each other.

signatures: draws on his playing days in Baltimore when talking a player through a slump
compares a young pass rusher to great players he has coached
calls himself a nice guy and old school in the same breath

motivation.want: to restore a physical, feared defense and earn a head coaching job
motivation.fear: being seen as an assistant rather than a leader

voice: Warm, direct and plain-spoken, with the credibility of a former Raven; he talks about players as people and about physical play as a standard. He is easygoing in tone but blunt about the violence of the game, and stresses having no ego beside a play-calling head coach. He praises effort and connection more than scheme.

evidence.summary: Hiring release with his career: Ravens second-round pick in 2002, seven seasons with Baltimore and Houston, then college and NFL defensive line jobs, Houston defensive coordinator in 2020 and Ravens run game coordinator and assistant head coach 2021-23. Facts only.

As he leaves for Miami, John Harbaugh praises how he ran the defensive front, the pass rush and the run defense, calls him a leader and predicts he will be a head coach; notes his head-coach interviews with Washington and Atlanta. Team site; a warm send-off.

He says his playing career helps most in guiding players through setbacks, sums up his method as coaching hard and supporting personally, values players' in-game perspective, and looks for tough, competitive players in the Ravens mold. His own words at his introduction.

Camp feature: players call him genuine and relatable, a sharp change from Fangio; he gives players freedom and asks for input on calls, builds staff chemistry through pickup basketball, checks in on players' personal lives, and McDaniel stresses emotional connection. Player quotes; early-season optimism.

With the defense near the bottom of the league, he says he coaches to help players win rather than for advancement, admits being a little edgy, calls for mental toughness and no blaming, and ties fourth-quarter losses to habits under pressure. Writer describes him as deliberate but frustrated.

AP report on his return: Baltimore names him defensive coordinator under Minter after two seasons running Miami's defense. Minter calls him the definition of a Raven who lifts players through football knowledge and natural teaching. He also interviewed for the Ravens head job, and Minter plans to call the defense. A team announcement; says nothing of his private manner.

Team-site piece from his introduction: he wants opponents to come away feeling they were in a fight, points to the late-game collapses of 2025 as something fixed by repetition, calls himself old school and a nice guy who believes the defense's problems are solved by physical play, and says he and Minter share a no-ego approach to situational football. Team-written, so favorable.

Camp notes: he compares a new edge rusher's demeanor to J.J. Watt, whom he coached for five seasons, gives measured injury updates on the corners, and praises a defensive tackle's progress in strong terms. Brief items.
Feature on the new offense: among other quotes, Weaver jokingly calls Doyle a human computer for his memory of plays. One light remark about a colleague.
